description: Xenon is team that will create smart tools for human spaceflight. We will be developing a visual tool for astronauts that will gather multimodal health information including keyboard inputs, ultrasound images, and real time biometrics such as blood sugar, heart rates,etc. This helps crews to manage their health effectively through converting complex health data into visual alerts, treatment plans and advice on how to improve their health.
summary: ASTRO-VITAL is a desktop computer program about health for astronauts. It is in Python - it has a native Tkinter interface. Every day crew members answer questions about their immune systems, bones and muscles, hearts and blood flow and thoughts plus feelings but also sleep and energy levels. The program uses those answers to make scores that have different colors to show if the user is ready. It also shows a warning if the user enters serious symptoms like chest pain or changes in their vision and it tells the user what they should do next. In addition the program has a place to record regular measurements - it has charts that show how those numbers change over time. Users have access to texts about how space travel harms human bodies, which are from NASA's Human Research Program. The program also has tools that tell users how to exercise and it counts how many consecutive days users open the program to make them continue to use it. The program doesn't have an internet connection, operates offline; people can use it during missions that take a long time, during which doctors on Earth are far away for travel time. This program is a preliminary model for training - it isn't a flight surgeon.
details:
ASTRO-VITAL: Project Details

What it does and how it works

ASTRO-VITAL is a desktop health companion that helps astronauts monitor their well-being during long missions. Each day, the crew member completes a short check-in covering five health areas: immunity, bones and muscles, heart and circulation, mind and mood, and sleep and energy. Their answers, along with a resting pulse and optional measurements, are converted into scores from 0 to 100 for each area and an overall readiness score.

Results are shown in four colors: green means all good, yellow means keep an eye on it, orange means take care and follow the advice, and red means contact the flight surgeon now. Each area comes with practical, context-specific advice. Urgent symptoms, such as chest pain, fainting, or sudden vision loss, trigger an immediate alert and cap the overall score.

Other features include:

Routine measurements (temperature, blood pressure, body mass, near vision) with trend charts and reference bands.

A learning library of 14 plain-language cards on spaceflight health risks, each linked to NASA’s Human Research Program.

An exercise coach that demonstrates movements and, with a webcam and optional libraries, counts repetitions and scores form.

Motivation features such as daily quests, XP and levels, badges, streaks with shields, a crew leaderboard, and streak buddies.

Benefits

Early warning. Trends over days can reveal problems, such as a falling sleep score or rising temperature, before they become serious.

Works offline. Everything runs on the local machine with no internet connection, which matters when communication with Earth is delayed or limited.

Clear, low-jargon guidance. Colors and plain-language advice help crew members act quickly without needing medical training.

Learning built in. Crew members can read about the risks they face, which supports informed self-care.

Engagement. Gamified habits encourage regular check-ins, hydration, and exercise, which NASA research identifies as important for crew health.

Intended impact

The app is designed to support crew health between medical contacts and to make it easier for crews to notice and report changes early. For mission planners and flight surgeons, the daily data can show patterns across a crew. More broadly, it can help the public understand the health challenges of spaceflight and inspire interest in space medicine.

The app is an educational prototype. It is not a medical device and does not replace a flight surgeon or clinical care.

Tools and technologies

Language: Python 3 (standard library only for the core app)

Interface: Tkinter, with custom canvas drawing for buttons, charts, and animations

Optional libraries: OpenCV and MediaPipe for pose detection in the exercise coach

Data storage: A local JSON file, with passwords protected by salted hashing (hashlib, hmac, secrets)

Development environment: Visual Studio Code

Hardware: Any standard computer. A webcam is needed only for the exercise coach.

Reference material: NASA Human Research Program pages on the five hazards, risks, and ongoing research

Creativity

Human-centered language. Questions and advice are written in everyday words instead of clinical terms, and the app avoids alarming wording where it isn’t needed.

Gamification with a purpose. Rewards focus on healthy habits rather than health results, so crew members aren’t ranked on their medical status.

Warm visual design. A custom dark theme, a mascot named Nova, and a rounded, friendly interface make a serious subject feel approachable.

Accessible exercise demonstrations. Animated figures show each movement, and the optional camera coach gives live feedback without needing a trainer.

A single-file design. The whole app is one Python file, so it can be shared, run, and studied easily.

Factors the team considered

Limited connectivity. The app works fully offline, since communication with Earth can be delayed or interrupted.

Privacy and safety. Data stays on the local device. Passwords are hashed, and the app avoids storing sensitive or diagnostic information beyond what is needed.

Accessibility of the platform. It needs only Python and Tkinter, so it runs on common computers without special hardware.

Crew wellbeing. Competition is kept friendly, with crew leaderboards based on healthy habits and not health results. Mental health prompts point to the behavioral health team and crisis support.

Scientific grounding. Health areas and risks follow NASA’s five hazards and identified risks, so the content reflects real research.

Since there was limited time and resources, ai was used for coding, debugging and troubleshooting yet the team members are the ones who does almost all the tasks which includes purposing ideas, madking the layout, building the app, debugging when necessary and refined and gave a final touch.

Honest limits. The app is clearly labeled as an educational prototype that does not replace medical care.
